A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system that helps websites load quickly no matter where a visitor is located. Normally, opening a website means requesting information from a single origin server — the main computer where the website's files are stored. If that server is far away, the request must travel a long distance, which takes time and can feel slow.

A CDN solves this by placing many copies of a website's content on servers scattered around the world. Each of these servers is called an edge location, because it sits at the edge of the network, close to where people actually are. When a visitor requests a page, the request goes to the nearest edge location instead of traveling all the way to the origin server.

If that nearby edge location already holds a saved copy of the requested content, this is called a cache hit — the content is delivered instantly without contacting the original source. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep copies of popular books, so people need not travel to one central library across the country every time they want to read something.

When there is no saved copy nearby, the edge location fetches it from the origin server once, then stores it for next time. This mix of nearby storage and smart routing is why CDN-powered websites tend to feel fast and reliable even during high traffic, since the workload spreads across many locations instead of overwhelming one single computer.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer where a website's files are stored | It is the ultimate source used when no nearby copy exists |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of website content | It shortens the distance information has to travel to reach a visitor |
| Cache hit | The moment a nearby copy already exists and gets served | It makes pages load almost instantly |
| Cache miss | The moment no nearby copy exists yet | It causes a slightly slower first request while a copy is fetched and stored for future use |
